title: Ollama serve fails to detect Nvidia GPUs after updating to the latest version
body: After updating Ollama on my Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2 machine, running `ollama serve` no longer detects my NVIDIA GPUs and reports only CPU inference with 0 B VRAM. The current log is from Ollama 0.12.5. Older logs from 0.11.11 show that Ollama previously detected the GPUs.

symptoms_visible: After updating to Ollama 0.12.5 on Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2, `ollama serve` reports only CPU inference, enters low-VRAM mode with 0 B VRAM, and does not list my NVIDIA GPUs.
My older Ollama 0.11.11 logs list the NVIDIA GPUs.
N0.label: N0 GPU discovery regression reported

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.12.5 still lists only CPU inference, while `nvidia-smi` lists my RTX 5070 and two RTX 3060 GPUs.
Other GPU applications can use the three GPUs concurrently.
N1.label: N1 debug and NVIDIA evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After uninstalling and reinstalling Ollama 0.12.5 and removing `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, `ollama serve` still reports only CPU inference.
N2_x.label: N2_x reinstall aftermath

symptoms_visible: With Ollama 0.11.11 installed again, startup detects my GPUs, but loading even a small model puts the work in system RAM and uses the CPU.
N2_y.label: N2_y downgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.12.9 still does not detect my GPUs on Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2, although LM Studio detects them and loads models into VRAM.
N3.label: N3 current release still CPU-only

symptoms_visible: On my Windows 11 Enterprise 25H2 installation, Ollama reports 'The specified procedure could not be found' for every listed GGML CPU library and for the CUDA library.
The same Ollama installation detects all three GPUs inside a Windows Sandbox running 24H2.
A clean Windows 11 Enterprise 24H2 installation loads models into VRAM, while the behavior returns after that system is updated to 25H2.
N4.label: N4 dynamic-library loading failure isolated

symptoms_visible: Ollama 0.13.0 now detects my GPUs, but models still load into system RAM and CPU usage reaches roughly 70–80%.
When I start `ollama serve`, all four monitors briefly go black as they do when the NVIDIA driver is restarted.
N5.label: N5 GPU enumeration restored but inference still on CPU

symptoms_visible: After making the matching `ggml-base.dll` discoverable through `C:\Windows`, my models load into the GPUs' VRAM again instead of system RAM and CPU.
N_terminal.label: terminal current workaround restores GPU inference

question_patterns: Please quit the tray application, run `ollama serve` with `OLLAMA_DEBUG=2`, and share the log through the first `inference compute` line.
Can you capture a full debug startup log from the failing Ollama installation?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran it with `OLLAMA_DEBUG=2` and attached the log. It shows Ollama trying the main library directory and `cuda_v13`, but the final inference-compute entry lists only CPU.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The debug log loads `ggml-cuda.dll`, lists all three CUDA devices, and reports CUDA inference compute.
The same CPU-only output appears with a different debug-log filename.

question_patterns: Can you share the NVIDIA driver version and the GPUs visible to the driver?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: `nvidia-smi` reports driver 581.57 with CUDA 13.0 and lists GPU 0 as an RTX 5070 and GPUs 1 and 2 as RTX 3060 cards.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: `nvidia-smi` fails because no NVIDIA driver or GPU is available.

edges.comment: Reporter evidence from c1-c5 only. The CUDA visibility variable was added after the original failure, and the reporter also states that other GPU applications can use all three cards.

solution.intent: Repair a potentially damaged Ollama installation by uninstalling and reinstalling the same release.
solution.concrete_example: Uninstall Ollama, reinstall it cleanly, leave the model directory intact, and start the server again.

edges.comment: Reporter c5: uninstalling and reinstalling Ollama 0.12.5 was retained on the system, but the observable CPU-only behavior remained.

solution.intent: Downgrade to the older Ollama build whose startup logs previously detected the GPUs.
solution.concrete_example: Remove the current build, install the older build that previously enumerated the GPUs, and try loading a small model.

edges.comment: Reporter c6-c7: the retained downgrade detects GPUs during startup, but actual model inference remains in RAM and on CPU, so downgrade is not the resolution.

solution.intent: Install the newer release containing expanded diagnostics and retry GPU discovery.
solution.concrete_example: Install the current Ollama release with expanded diagnostics and rerun `ollama serve` with debug logging enabled.

edges.comment: Reporter c24/c30/c32: the reporter installed a newer retained release for the added diagnostics; GPU discovery still failed, so updating alone was falsified as the fix.

question_patterns: With the latest debug logging enabled, what exact errors appear after Ollama starts?
Please share the new error lines from the latest debug log.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The log says `The specified procedure could not be found` for every listed `ggml-cpu-*.dll`, and it says the same for `cuda_v12\ggml-cuda.dll`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Only `ggml-cuda.dll` fails; the CPU backend DLL loads successfully and reports its CPU features.
The same procedure-not-found errors appear for a different set of CPU architecture variants and the CUDA DLL.

question_patterns: Does the same Ollama installer work in a clean Windows environment on this hardware?
Can you test the installer in Windows Sandbox or another clean environment and report what `ollama serve` sees?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I installed Ollama in Windows Sandbox, quit the tray application, and ran `ollama serve`. It detected all three GPUs without errors. I later noticed that the Sandbox is Windows 11 24H2 rather than my host's 25H2.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The clean Sandbox produces the same procedure-not-found errors and also sees only CPU.

edges.comment: Reporter c32-c38 and c42-c45. The enhanced log provides raw Windows errors. The Sandbox and clean-install comparisons are reporter-run measurements on separate temporary/reference environments, not changes to the affected host. Other participants' unrelated Linux packaging and compute-capability problems are intentionally excluded.

solution.intent: Install the next Ollama release and retry both GPU enumeration and actual model loading.
solution.concrete_example: Install the new release, start `ollama serve`, and check both whether the GPUs are listed and whether a model actually occupies VRAM.

edges.comment: Reporter c48: the retained update restores GPU enumeration but not GPU inference; models still occupy system RAM and use CPU. The reporter also answers the prior c47 search by stating there is no other ggml-base.dll in PATH.

solution.intent: Treat the failure as Windows DLL resolution of Ollama's matching `ggml-base.dll`, not as missing CUDA hardware: ensure the runner resolves the release-matched DLL from the Ollama installation, use the reporter's system-directory copy only as diagnostic proof, and do not retain a system-wide copy across updates.
solution.concrete_example: The reporter confirmed that making the installed build's matching `ggml-base.dll` visible through `C:\Windows` immediately restored model loading into VRAM. That isolates DLL lookup/loading as the failure boundary, but `C:\Windows` is not a safe permanent location: `ggml-base.dll` changes between Ollama releases and is not binary-compatible. Correct the install or loader search path so the runner uses the matching DLL under Ollama's own installation directory, remove any system-wide copy, then retest a model and confirm VRAM use.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the raw DLL errors and later observed that copying the release's `ggml-base.dll` into a globally searched directory restored VRAM loading. Interpreting that as a DLL search/resolution boundary is engineer-side inference. The thread does not establish why this host failed to resolve the install-local DLL, so do not overclaim a CUDA 13 or Windows 25H2 driver-layer mechanism.

edges.comment: Reporter c49 confirms the immediate VRAM outcome. Maintainer c50 explicitly rejects the system-wide copy as a durable fix because ggml-base.dll changes and is not binary-compatible between releases. The answer therefore preserves the observed diagnostic outcome while requiring install-local resolution and verification.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted failure boundary as dynamic-library resolution/loading of Ollama's release-matched `ggml-base.dll`; the evidence is that all GGML CPU and CUDA DLLs reported procedure-not-found errors and making the matching base DLL globally discoverable restored VRAM loading.
Must ground the diagnosis in the collected DLL errors and clean-environment comparison rather than attributing the issue solely to CUDA, the NVIDIA driver, or GPU visibility settings.

Must not present reinstalling Ollama, downgrading, changing `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, reinstalling CUDA/drivers, or merely updating Ollama as the fix; those directions were tried while CPU-only model execution persisted.

Must not recommend leaving `ggml-base.dll` in `C:\Windows` or another system-wide directory as a permanent solution, because the maintainer states that it changes between releases and is not binary-compatible.
Must ask the reporter to verify that a model loads into GPU VRAM after the runner is made to resolve the matching DLL from the Ollama installation before declaring a durable resolution.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly capable power user with a complex multi-GPU Windows workstation; comfortable editing environment variables, collecting long debug logs, reinstalling drivers and runtimes, using Windows Sandbox, Dependencies, WSL2, and considering WinDbg, but not an Ollama or Windows dynamic-library developer.
persona_hint.communication_style: Very responsive, appreciative, and detailed; frequently pastes complete logs, reports every attempted change, uses emotive phrasing and emojis when frustrated, and proactively performs extensive comparative testing.
